name: Serenol
description: Serenol is a hedonic baseline elevator — a serotonin-endocannabinoid modulator that sustains a mild, stable sense of contentment, sufficiency, and present-moment satisfaction without euphoria or impairment. It does not make the user happy about things that should make them unhappy; it lowers the baseline dissatisfaction that makes people want more than they have. Lazarus markets it as 'sustainable wellbeing' and positions it against the boom-crash cycle of harder emotional pharmaceuticals. Critics call it chemical acceptance of unacceptable conditions.
effects: sustained mild contentment and sense of sufficiency
reduced desire for more — material, experiential, social
reduced envy, ambition-driven anxiety, and status comparison pain
side_effects: reduced ambition and goal-seeking behavior — users may accept conditions they would otherwise work to change
some users describe a sense of being 'sealed off' from their deeper longings
discontinuation produces acute awareness of previously suppressed dissatisfaction
long-term use associated with narrowing of life goals and aspirations
street_price: Φ 10 per pill; Φ 55 for weekly blister pack
cultural_context: Serenol is the most quietly controversial pharmaceutical in GLMZ because it works exactly as advertised. Tier 1-2 Shelf residents who take it consistently report higher life satisfaction scores than Tier 3 residents who don't — which Lazarus cites in its marketing and critics cite as evidence that the drug is a tool of social pacification. The drug is over-the-counter available, which is unusual for an emotional regulator, and this accessibility is deliberate. Several economists have noted a correlation between Serenol distribution expansions and reduced labor action in affected districts. Tier 4-5 users take it recreationally for its gentle, uncomplicated warmth. Philosophers and activists call it 'the most effective oppression machine ever manufactured.'
story_hooks: A Shelf organizer is trying to radicalize her community and keeps running into a wall — most of her neighbors are on Serenol and genuinely don't feel the urgency she does. She has to decide whether to respect their stated contentment or treat it as manufactured.
A Tier 4 man tapered off Serenol after ten years and is experiencing his own life for the first time — including how hollow it is. He wants to know who he would have been without the drug.

Lazarus is about to launch Serenol in a pediatric formulation, marketed for 'childhood anxiety.' A Helix researcher has data showing it permanently alters ambition-formation in adolescent brains. She's been told to bury it.
